chunks.text:
Hi Kelly,
We see each other at events. That’s about it. That’s the arrangement, and there’s something honest about it.
Some friendships happen in the spaces between: conferences, parties, hackathons, those moments where you’re both in the same room and the conversation picks up like it never stopped. A “we cross paths and it still works” friendship.
I think that shape is underrated. We’re scattered across cities and time zones. The friendships that survive are the ones that can go dormant and reactivate without losing the thread. Last year I wrote about our friendship as a web, borrowing Adrienne Maree Brown’s image: catching what matters, letting the rest fall through. That still feels right.
Your piece, “when two people become close,” nails something I’ve been circling for years: how closeness can be real without being constant.1 The intimacy is about what happens when you’re actually in the room together, more than how often. Does the conversation go somewhere real? With us, it always has, since the hackathons and chance adjacency that somehow produced an actual friendship.

Ava argues in “the friendship theory of everything” that “in choosing who you spend time with you choose who you are.”2 It’s a heavy claim, but I think she’s right.
The part that stuck the most is a tweet she quotes, about a close friend becoming “the primary person who explains you to you.” The people who’ve watched you long enough to see the patterns, who believe you’ll be okay even when you don’t. That’s a form of redemption, she says: “if you have people who believe you’re going to be okay you believe that you’re going to be okay.”
When we ask for more from friendship, we also get more disappointment, conflict, mismatch. There is no such thing as closeness without friction.Ava, The Friendship Theory of Everything
I think about that line when I think about the friendships that last, where disappointment becomes part of the relationship instead of ending it. We haven’t had much friction, you and I. Maybe that’s because we don’t see each other enough to generate it. Or maybe it’s because we both understand the shape of what we have (recurring, durable, not needy) and we’re not trying to make it into something it isn’t.

I love seeing you do well, even from the periphery. Toronto has wrapped around you in a way that feels earned. You’ve found your rhythm here, and watching it happen, even in glimpses, has been one of the pleasures of this year.
It’s wild to think the HTN-era version of us was mostly vibes and chance adjacency. We were strangers who happened to be in the same digital room, and then we weren’t strangers anymore. We didn’t schedule calls or force consistency, but every time we crossed paths, something real happened. The thread held.
Last year I quoted Montaigne on his friendship with Étienne de La Boétie: “we sought one another long before we met.”3 I don’t know if that’s true for us. I’m not sure we were seeking anything. But when we found each other, it clicked.

I’m grateful for you. And I’m looking forward to the next event, the next conversation that picks up like it never stopped.
Here’s to another year of the web catching what matters.

remarque


kelly, “when two people become close”. your own piece on the mechanics of closeness: how it happens, what it requires, why it sometimes doesn’t. ↩


ava, “the friendship theory of everything”. the argument that friends shape us even more than romantic partners do, and that “the most important thing is that you both keep coming back.” ↩


michel de montaigne, “of friendship,” essays book I, ch. 28 (1580), in charles cotton’s translation. the essay about his friendship with la boétie is one of the great documents of what friendship can be, and what it costs to lose. ↩
